Zhao let him say all of them. He sat behind the desk and listened. The lawyer had a good suit. The hotel man had a gold watch he kept touching. Bao stood by the door eating sunflower seeds out of a paper bag, which he did when he was bored, which was a bad sign for somebody.

When the hotel man ran out of words, Zhao asked how many buildings he owned in the Walled City.

“Three. Two now, apparently.”

“Two.”

“And I’ll be building on both of them, Mr. Zhao, whatever—”

“No.”

Just that. The hotel man waited for the rest of the sentence. There wasn’t one. Zhao looked at him. Bao cracked a seed. The lawyer understood first. He put his papers back in his briefcase one sheet at a time.

They came down the stairs forty minutes after they’d gone up. Within the year the hotel man had sold both his other buildings and moved his business south. Nobody could get him to say why.

Aurelia told Elowen the whole thing over the phone a month later. Aurelia heard everything.

“Forty minutes, darling. He came out grey. What did your husband do?”

Elowen looked across the kitchen at her husband, who was watering the lemon tree because his phone had told him to.

“I think he said no.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop was shut six days. She ran orders out of Bao’s car and a borrowed cooler in the guardhouse. She walked past the shop twice a day anyway. She couldn’t help it. She’d stand on the pavement watching her brother in a hard hat and a paint-spattered hoodie wave at three builders like a rich boy who’d got lost on the way to a party.

He knew exactly what he was doing. She’d known that since he was ten, and turned up at the red door at eleven at night in a fish man’s coat that came down to his ankles. A map drawn on his arm in biro. Alone. Across a border.

The builders didn’t know. To them he was the boss’s silly brother-in-law who sang along to the radio and forgot their names. They didn’t see him check every weld himself after they went home. They didn’t see him in the empty shop at midnight with a torch and a tape, walking the floor. Door to hatch. Hatch to cooler. Cooler to the back exit. Over and over, till he could do it blind.

Zhao saw.

On the fourth night she brought a flask of soup down at eleven, and found both of them there. Raiden on an upturned bucket with a drawing on his knees. Zhao standing over the open hatch, looking down into the dark.

Neither of them heard her. She stopped in the doorway.

“Two metres by three.” Raiden’s real voice. Lower. Flatter. A lot like Baba’s. “Steel plate under the concrete. The hatch looks like a drain cover. Second row of buckets. Tulips. She always keeps tulips there. I checked three years of her order books.”

“Air?”

“Pipe up inside the wall. Comes out above the cooler vent, where nobody looks. Water for three days. A phone line through the building next door, not this one. Eliana’s doing the alarm. She says the shop will ring you before anyone outside knows something’s wrong.”

Zhao nodded at the hole.

“You’ve built these before.”

“Four. For Baba.” Raiden drew a careful line. “And I was in one, once. At the farm. A chest freezer in the kitchen. There were trucks on the river road one night, and my uncle took the food out and put me in.”

Zhao turned his head. Raiden didn’t look up.

“Eleven hours.” The pencil kept going. “I counted. To forty thousand. Every thousand I made a mark on my hand with my fingernail. In the dark.”

“Did they come?”

“No.” He almost smiled at the paper. “Nobody came. That was sort of the point.”

Zhao didn’t say anything. Then he crouched down on the other side of the hatch, so they were level, with the black hole between them.

“Make it bigger. Not two by three. So she can lie down.” A beat. “And a light. A good one. Not a torch. A light that stays on.”

Raiden looked up.

“That’ll cost more.”

“I know.”

They looked at each other across the hole in her floor. Her brother, who’d counted to forty thousand in a freezer. Her husband, who’d held a man’s hands over a fire.

Raiden put the pencil behind his ear. “Okay. A light that stays on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She should’ve gone in then. She knew it. She stood there with the flask going cold in her hands. Twelve years he’d been home. Twelve years, and she’d never once heard him say the word freezer.

Raiden put the pencil down.

“Can I ask you something?”

Zhao waited.

“Do you love her?”

Plain. No silly voice. A brother on a bucket in the middle of the night.

Her hand locked on the flask.

“Yes.”

No pause. None. The way other men said their own names.

She had to put a hand flat on the doorframe.

“Have you told her?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

Zhao stood up. He walked to the counter where a bucket of eucalyptus had been left behind, and stood looking at it with his back to the room.

“She married me to protect your father. If I say it, she’ll say it back.” He touched one leaf. “Because she’s kind. Because that’s what she does. I don’t want it because she’s kind. I don’t want it because she thinks she owes me.”

“So you’ll never tell her. Ever.”

“I’ll wait. Till I know she’d say it even if I didn’t.”

“And how will you know?”

Zhao didn’t answer.

Raiden picked his pencil back up. When he spoke again it was in his normal bright voice. Like nothing had happened.

“You know, for a really frightening man, you’re extremely stupid.”

Zhao turned round.

“My sister has looked after all of us since she was seven. She’s never done one thing in her life just for herself. Not the shop. The shop was for Elara’s school fees.” He shaded something. “Not the physics boy. She liked him because he was quiet and she was tired.”

“And me.”

“And you. I thought, okay. Same thing. Another thing she’s doing for somebody else.”

“It is.”

“It was.” Raiden looked up. “Then she was late to Sunday lunch last month because she’d been on a mountain. Looking at a flower. Her flower. Her mountain. She talked about it for an hour, Zhendong. She was happy. Not looking-after-us happy. Happy for her.” Back to the drawing. “Haven’t seen that since Mama died. I’m only a draftsman. But if I were a frightening, stupid arms dealer, I might think about it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen backed out of the doorway without a sound. She walked to the end of the street and stood under the lamp with the flask. Her heart was going so hard she could feel it in her teeth.

Yes.

He’d said yes. To her brother. In the middle of the night, over a hole in her floor. Not to her.

Till I know she’d say it even if I didn’t.

What was she supposed to do with that? Walk back in and say it? He’d think she only said it because she’d heard. Of course he would.

She walked back. Loudly this time. Scuffing her shoes. She shouldered the door open.

“I brought soup. It’s cold now. That’s your fault, Raiden, you should’ve finished by ten!”

Her brother looked up from his bucket with big innocent eyes. He didn’t look at the doorway at all. Oh, the little rat. He’d seen her there the whole time.

Zhao took the flask out of her hands.

“You walked here. Alone. At eleven at night.”

“Bao was across the road.”

He looked at her. She looked back. I heard you. I heard every word. She took the flask back and poured him a cup of cold soup and put it in his hands.

“It’s cold but it’s still soup. You haven’t eaten since lunch.”

He drank it standing up. All of it. Then he put the cup down and looked at her coat. It was hanging open. It was cold out.

“Can I?”

The zip. He was asking about the zip. Seven months married. He’d seen every scar she had, and she’d seen all of his, and he still asked about the zip.

“You don’t have to ask for that any more.”

“I know.”

He asked anyway. He waited. She nodded. He zipped her coat up to her chin, slowly, like he was posting her somewhere safe.

“Next time you walk anywhere alone after ten, I carry you.”

“You can’t carry me through the Walled City.”

“Hm. I’d like to see someone stop me.”

“Please don’t. I have to live there.” From the bucket.

Elowen didn’t look at her brother. She took the front of her husband’s coat in both fists and pulled him down by it and kissed him.

She meant it to be quick. It wasn’t. She was thinking about yes, said over a hole in the floor in the voice other men used for their names. She couldn’t say any of it out loud. So she said it this way. Until his hand came up to the back of her neck and she forgot there was anyone else in the shop.

When she let go he was looking at her like he was trying to work out what he’d done to deserve it.

Behind them, Raiden had put the drawing over his face.

“I’m a draftsman,” he said from under it. “I’m not here. I’m a bucket.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The shop opened again on Sunday. The new floor was warm under her feet, pale grey, smooth as a pebble. There was a new drain cover under the second row of buckets, where the tulips always were. You’d never know.

On Monday, before anyone came in, she moved the tulips and lifted it. A ladder went down into a room big enough to lie down in. Blankets. Water. A phone on the wall. And when her foot touched the bottom rung, a light came on by itself. Warm. Steady. Bright. Like a lamp left on in a window for somebody coming home late.

She sat down there in that light for a while. On the wall by the phone, somebody had taped a small piece of paper. Square, blunt capitals she’d have known anywhere. Two lines.

This light stays on.

I’ll come.

chapters.title: A Reunion Invitation With One Name on It
chapters.desc: The school turns sixty and Miles Wei is giving the speech. At two in the morning she finds her husband reading his papers.
chapters.epigraph: “The Harbour Hotel. Black tie. And darling, read the second page.” — Aurelia Chen
chapters.content:
“Have you opened it?”

“Opened what?”

“Don’t what me. The invitation. Thick white card. Gold crest. Sixty years of our dear old school. Every year invited.” Aurelia was clearly lying on something soft. “The fourteenth of December. The Harbour Hotel. Black tie. And darling, read the second page.”

Elowen was wiring a funeral wreath. She put the wire down. The envelope was on the counter where Xiao Pan had left the post. She slit it with her florist’s knife.

A card. A folded sheet behind it.

Programme for the evening. Reception. Dinner. Then an address by a distinguished former student: Dr. Miles Wei, Lecturer in Physics, City University. “Light, and Other Things That Bend.”

She read it twice.

On the other end of the phone, Aurelia was laughing so hard she had to stop and breathe.

“He’s going to bend light at us. For half an hour. In a hotel ballroom. Seven years later!”

A shriek. Something fell off a sofa.

“I’m on the committee. Did I tell you? Everything’s going to be gold. I’ve bought a gold dress. I’m going to match the ceiling and sit in the front row and not blink once.”

“I’m not going.”

“Of course you’re going.”

“I’ve got a big order the next morning. Two hundred arrangements.”

“You’ve had a big order every morning for five years and you still came to my launch.” Aurelia’s voice changed. Lower. Sharper. “Are you scared?”

“Of Miles?”

“Of your husband. Seeing Miles.”

Elowen looked down at the card. Dr. Miles Wei.

She thought about Baba in the dining room. You were only the price she paid. She thought about the basement. I know. Flat. Finished.

“I’ll call you back.”

“Elowen, don’t you DARE hang up on—”

She hung up.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t mention it at dinner. She meant to. She opened her mouth three times and talked about the funeral wreath instead.

In the morning she left the invitation on the kitchen counter, under the bowl of mandarins, and said nothing. She was a coward. Also, if he found it on his own, he could decide what to feel without her watching his face.

When she came home that evening, it had moved.

It was beside the mandarins now. Squared exactly to the edge of the counter. Second page on top.

He was at the stove. Noodles. He’d learned this month. Badly at first. Then less badly. Now he made them most nights she worked late, very seriously, with her recipe propped against the salt.

“You found it.”

“You put it under the mandarins.”

The spring onions on the board were cut on a sharp diagonal. Every piece the same length. Lined up in a row like soldiers.

“You cut them on the angle.”

“More surface.” He didn’t turn round. “It drinks the sauce better.”

Her line. The first night, in the rain, about roses. He’d kept it all this time. Where did he keep all these things?

She sat on the stool.

“I don’t have to go.”

He turned off the heat. Two bowls. He put one in front of her, sat on the other stool, and looked at her.

“Do you want to?”

She thought about it properly. He deserved that.

“I want to watch Aurelia lose her mind in a gold dress. I want to see the teachers. A couple of them were kind to me when Mama died.” She stopped. “And I want to see if he’s the same. Miles. I don’t know why. He was the only one at that school who didn’t look at me and see Baba.”

Zhao looked at his noodles.

“Then go.”

“Will you come?”

His chopsticks stopped.

“To your school reunion.”

“Partners are invited. Look.” She turned the card over. Plus one, in gold. “Aurelia’s bringing Chen Si. I don’t want to walk in on my own. Please?”

“I don’t dance.”

“Nobody in my year dances. We were very serious students.”

He looked at her. She saw it again for a second. The stone under the quilt.

“All right.”

She texted Aurelia under the table before he could change his mind.

Elowen: he’s coming

Aurelia: who

Elowen: my husband

Aurelia: TO THE REUNION??

Elowen: plus one. it says so on the card

Aurelia: oh my god. oh my GOD. I’m moving you to table nine

Elowen: what’s at table nine

Aurelia: me

Aurelia: and a very good view of the stage

She put the phone face down. Too late. He’d read it upside down. He read everything upside down.

“Table nine?”

“She’s on the committee. She’s drunk on power.”

“Hm.” He picked his chopsticks back up. “Where’s the stage?”

“Zhendong.”

“I want to know where the exits are.”

She looked at him. He looked at his noodles. He was not asking about exits. Who did he think he was fooling?

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning she woke up, and his side of the bed was empty.

No basement door. She waited for the metal clunk of the lock. It didn’t come. There was a strip of light under the door from the corridor.

She got up.

He was in the little room at the top of the stairs. The one he’d slept in for the first month, between her and the stairs. He was sitting on the narrow bed with his laptop on his knees, and the screen was full of maths.

Not numbers. Maths. Integrals. Greek letters. Equations that ran the whole width of the page.

He was frowning at it like a gun he’d never seen before. At the top of the page:

Gravitational lensing of light by low-mass compact objects: a perturbative approach. M. Wei, City University.

She didn’t know whether to laugh or cry.

“Zhendong.”

He shut the laptop so hard it went off like a shot.

They looked at each other.

“I couldn’t sleep.”

“You’re reading Miles Wei’s research papers.”

“One.”

There was a stack of printouts on the bed beside him. Three. One had notes in the margin in his square, blunt writing. She could read one upside down. It said: ?

“Three.”

He looked at the stack. He didn’t argue.

She sat down next to him. The narrow bed creaked. She picked up the top paper. Next to an equation six lines long he’d written: What is this. A few lines down: Light bends because of mass. Heavy things pull it. And under that, smaller, like he’d written it later: She said he talked about how light bends.

She put it down.

“Did you understand any of it?”

“No.” At the closed laptop. “The first paragraph. Something very heavy, like a star, makes light from behind it go round it instead of straight. So you see the thing in the wrong place.” A pause. “I read it eleven times.”

“Eleven.”

“Why?”

He took a long time.

“I wanted to know what you liked about him. You said he was quiet. You said he talked about light. I thought, if I knew what he knew, I’d understand what you…” He stopped. “I don’t know. It was stupid.”

“It was.”

He looked at her.

“Very stupid.” She was smiling now. Her eyes were wet. “You sat up at two in the morning and read about light going round a star eleven times because you thought that’s what I wanted.”

“Isn’t it?”

She took the laptop off his knees and put it on the floor. The papers on top. Then she took his face in both hands.

“I liked Miles because he was quiet. I was seventeen. I had a brother and three sisters and a father who was frightened all the time.”

“I know.”

“A house full of people who wanted something from me. He was the only one who didn’t want anything. He wanted physics. He didn’t even want me.” She held his face. “That’s what I liked. It was restful.”

“I want everything.” Low. “I’m not restful.”

“No. You’re not.” She put her forehead on his. “You sit outside my door. You buy mountains. You bled on two hundred roses.”

“A hundred and eighty.”

“You read physics at two in the morning because you’re jealous of a man I haven’t spoken to in seven years.” Her voice cracked. “Nobody’s ever wanted me that much. It’s not restful at all. It’s terrifying.”

“Then why are you smiling?”

She didn’t answer. She kissed him.

He made a low noise and pulled her into his lap. The narrow bed groaned. The printouts slid off the laptop and went all over the floor. Gravitational lensing. Perturbative approach. Who cared? She pushed him down on the narrow bed in the smallest room in the house and kissed him till he stopped thinking about light.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, after he’d gone down to make coffee, she picked the papers up off the floor and put them in order.

She read his margins. All of them. What is this. Mass bends light. She said he talked about light. And on the very last page, at the bottom, under a final equation he clearly hadn’t understood either, one line. He must have written it just before she came in.

He made her feel calm. I make her feel afraid. I should let her go to the reunion alone.

She sat on the narrow bed and looked at it for a long time.

Then she found a pen on the bedside table and wrote underneath, in her small neat wedding-card writing:

No. You come with me. Plus one.

And for the record, I said terrifying. That isn’t the same as afraid.

She left it on his pillow in their room.

✦ ✦ ✦

Bao put the folder on his desk at the Docks on Wednesday.

“You said everything.”

“Yes.”

“It isn’t much, boss.”

Zhao opened it. One photograph off a university website. Thin. Glasses. Hair sticking up at the back. A list. A flat behind the university sports ground. Lives alone. No car. No debts. No girlfriend anyone could find. A parking fine from three years ago, paid on time. Plants on the windowsill. The cleaner said cactuses.

“Cactuses.”

“Three. And one on the doormat. She doesn’t know why.”

Zhao read every line. Then he read it again. Somewhere in a calm, far-off room in his head, he was working out how long it would take to drive from the Docks to the sports ground at night. Twenty minutes. Fifteen, without traffic. It didn’t mean anything. It was just a number. He liked to know the numbers.

“How does he get to work?”

Bao looked at the list.

“The bus.”

Zhao closed the folder.

The physics boy took the bus. Still. Seven years and he was still taking the bus. Zhao sat with his hand flat on the cardboard and felt something in his chest loosen and something else tighten, and didn’t know which was worse.

Terrifying isn’t the same as afraid. Her writing. In his pocket. He’d read it more times than the paper.

“Boss? You want anything else on him?”

“No.”

He put the folder in the bottom drawer. He locked it. He put the key on the ring with her van keys.

Bao, to the window: “Nothing. He wants nothing. Right.”

Then, because she couldn’t help it, she took the other two papers down to the shop and read them at the counter between customers. She understood almost nothing. She liked the pictures. Galaxies stretched into rings. One star showing up four times.

Xiao Pan read the title over her shoulder.

“Miss Lin. Is this homework?”

“Sort of.”

“Is it for Mr. Zhao?”

“Why would it be for Mr. Zhao?”

Xiao Pan looked at the paper. Then at her face. Then he went very red and said he’d do the deliveries early today.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t mention the note.

But that night the page was gone from his pillow. And on Saturday he took her to a dress shop on Harbour Road she’d walked past for years without going in.

“I have dresses!”

“You have one dress. It’s green. You wore it to a man getting stabbed.”

She opened her mouth. He had a point. She shut it again.

The woman in the shop took one look at him and went pale.

“Does madam have a… a budget in mind?”

“Yes.” Elowen, fast.

“No.” Zhao sat down.

“Yes. I have a budget. It’s—”

“No.”

The woman looked from one to the other and brought out everything she had. Elowen tried on five. He sat in a gold chair outside the changing room with her handbag on his knee, upright, both hands on it, like he was guarding it from the other customers.

The blue one. “Hm.”

The black one. “Hm.”

The silver one, with the low back. A long, long “Hm.”

“That’s not a word, Zhendong. Is it good? Is it bad? Blink twice!”

The fifth one was red.

She came out in it and he didn’t say anything at all. Not hm. Nothing. He just looked at her, sitting very still with her handbag on his knee. For so long the shop woman started to sweat.

“Well?”

He stood up.

“That one.” To the woman. “And the other four.”

“I’m not wearing five dresses to one reunion—”

“Not to the reunion.” He took his wallet out of his inside pocket. “To everything after.”

When he opened his jacket she saw it. Folded small. Tucked behind the wallet, in the left pocket where he kept her three pages.

The corner of Miles Wei’s last page. With her writing on it.

He had no idea she’d seen. She wasn’t going to tell him. Not ever.

She went back in to change with her face hot and her heart going stupid, and stood in front of the mirror in the red dress for a whole minute, just breathing.

chapters.title: Zhao Zhendong Is Absolutely Fine About the Physics Lecturer
chapters.desc: Zhao borrows Xiao Pan's FLOWER POWER hoodie and goes to the physics lecture in disguise. Chen Si finds him at the back.
chapters.epigraph: “I am completely fine.” — Zhao Zhendong, to nobody, eleven times
chapters.content:
Zhao did not read the evening paper. Except that one Tuesday he did.

FREE PUBLIC LECTURE. “Why the Universe Lies to Us About Where Things Are.” Dr. Miles Wei. Thursday, 7 p.m., Lecture Theatre B. All welcome.

He read it three times. He found Lecture Theatre B on the university map. Then every car park within walking distance of it. Then he folded the paper very small and put it in the bin in the garage. Under an empty oil can. Where his wife would never, ever look.

On Thursday he told her he had a meeting in the north of the city.

It wasn’t a lie. He’d made sure. That afternoon he rang a broker in the north called Hou and set up fifteen minutes at ten, about nothing. So when he said I have a meeting, it was true.

He told himself this was keeping the contract.

He knew perfectly well it wasn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t own a hoodie. He’d thought about this. A man in a dark coat at the back of a lecture theatre looked like a man in a dark coat. A man in a hoodie looked like a student. Students were invisible.

So on Thursday morning, at the shop, while Elowen was out at the bank, he went to the back room.

“Xiao Pan.”

The boy dropped a bucket.

“Yes, Mr. Zhao! Sorry. Yes. Hello.”

“Can I borrow your hoodie?”

Xiao Pan looked down at himself. The grey one. He always wore the grey one.

“This one?”

“Yes.”

“…Yes. Okay. Yes.” Xiao Pan took it off. He handed it over like a flag at a funeral. “You can have it. You don’t have to give it back.”

“I’ll give it back.”

Zhao folded it under his arm and went to the door. He had the door open when the boy’s voice came after him, very small.

“Mr. Zhao? It says FLOWER POWER on the back.”

“I know.”

He left anyway.

Xiao Pan stood in the back room in his T-shirt and made a decision. He would not ask any more questions. Not today. Possibly not for the rest of his life.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lecture Theatre B was enormous. And full.

He’d pictured a small room. Twenty students. Instead: three hundred seats in steep rows, nearly every one taken. Students with laptops. Old men with notebooks. A class of schoolgirls in uniform. A woman in the aisle seat, knitting.

He came in five minutes late in the grey hoodie and a cap pulled low, and stood at the very back against the wall by the door.

The man on the stage was thin. Thinner than Zhao had pictured. Dark glasses frames. A grey jumper with a hole in one elbow. Hair sticking up at the back like he’d been dragging his hands through it. He was holding a clicker for the slides and looked like he’d forgotten what it did.

“So.” Into the microphone. “I want to start with a question. Can you trust your own eyes?”

Three hundred people waited.

“No. Not if you’re looking at the sky.”

Click. A bright yellow blob on the screen, and four smaller blobs round it in a cross.

“This is one quasar. One. Ten billion light years away. You can see four of it. Why?”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao had come ready to hate him.

He’d read the three papers eleven times each. He’d understood one paragraph. He’d stood in the shower that morning and decided what kind of man made his wife smile like that, seven years later, without meaning to. Clever. Cold. Careless with people. A man who’d looked at two seventeen-year-old girls fighting over him and picked physics, because physics didn’t need anything.

He stood at the back and listened. And slowly, against his will, he understood.

The man didn’t make you feel small. That was the worst part. He made the universe sound like a secret he was telling you personally. He talked too fast and then stopped and said sorry and went back and said it slower. He drew on the screen with his finger. He went pink in the face about a picture of a galaxy bent into a ring.

A schoolgirl in the third row put her hand up. A good question. He stopped the whole lecture for five minutes and answered her properly. When she got it, he looked so delighted the whole theatre laughed.

Then he dropped the clicker.

“Sorry. Sorry! Hang on…”

He went under the lectern after it, still talking into the microphone.

“…so, something very heavy bends the space round it. And light doesn’t get a choice. It has to follow the shape.” He came back up, glasses crooked. “Light from something far behind comes round it, instead of straight to you. So you see the thing in the wrong place. Or four times. Or as a ring.”

He drew a circle on the screen.

“The heavy thing in the middle, you can’t see at all. You only know it’s there because of how everything round it bends.”

Zhao stood very still against the back wall.

A fish belly, going round a table three times between three people.

A lemon tree with five lemons. It had only ever had three.

A woman on a mountain in the rain. I’m happy. I didn’t know I wasn’t.

You only know it’s there because of how everything round it bends.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re wearing a hoodie that says FLOWER POWER.”

Zhao didn’t turn his head.

“How long have you been there?”

“Since the quasar.” Chen Si leaned on the wall beside him. Camel coat. Hands in pockets. Polite interest, aimed at the stage. “Bao rang me. He was worried. He said you’d borrowed a teenager’s clothes, told your wife you had a meeting, and driven yourself to a university. He thought you might be having a breakdown.”

“I’m fine.”

“Of course you are.”

“Go home, Si.”

“And miss this?” Chen Si nodded at the stage. “He’s about to do black holes. I’ve always wanted to know about black holes.”

On the stage, the clicker went again. The theatre laughed.

“He’s not what I expected,” Zhao said, after a while.

“No. He’s nice. That’s very annoying, isn’t it.”

Zhao didn’t answer.

“Aurelia told me about him on our second date.” Chen Si watched the stage. “The only thing she ever wanted and didn’t get, she said. She said it like he was a necklace. She doesn’t love him. She loves that she couldn’t have him.” A sideways look. “Is that what you’re afraid of? That Elowen’s the same?”

“No.”

“Then what?”

Miles Wei was drawing another ring of light with his finger, beaming at it.

“That she’d have been happy.” Low. “With someone like that. Quiet. Kind. Libraries. Nobody shooting at her. A man she didn’t need a contract for.” He stopped. “That I took it off her.”

Chen Si was quiet for a while.

“Zhendong. I’ve seen you scared twice. Once in Block C, when you thought I was dead. And now.” He took his hands out of his pockets. “Both times you were wrong.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know a woman who wanted a quiet life with a physics lecturer doesn’t walk into the Iron Docks with three pages of terms.” He straightened his coat. “Come on. I’ll buy you dinner. You can’t see your broker in that. You look like a delinquent.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He saw the broker in it anyway.

Hou was round and cheerful. He’d been late with a payment since summer and thought nobody had noticed. He started to laugh when Zhao sat down across from him with FLOWER POWER on his back.

“Nice… jumper, Mr. Zhao.”

“Hm.”

“Is it… is it a new look? Very young. Very fresh.”

Then he saw Zhao’s face. He stopped laughing.

Zhao put his hands flat on the table and said nothing. For most of fifteen minutes. Hou talked. About the port. His wife’s health. The price of diesel. His shirt went dark under the arms. Then dark down the back.

At the end Zhao said one word.

“Friday.”

Hou paid the next morning. Afterwards he told people the hoodie was the worst part. A man who dressed like that to come and see you plainly didn’t care what you thought of him. And a man who didn’t care what you thought could do anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came home at midnight.

He’d changed in the car. Shirt back on. Hoodie and cap on the back seat. Nobody would ever know.

She was in the kitchen on one of the tall stools with a cup of tea. On the counter in front of her, laid out flat like evidence, were a cap and a grey hoodie with FLOWER POWER across the back in yellow.

He stopped in the doorway.

Behind him, Bao came in from the car, put the car keys in the bowl, and went straight back out again.

“Bao brought them in,” Elowen said. “Five minutes ago. He said, Mrs. Zhao, I think these are evidence, and left.”

“Bao.”

From outside, very faint, through the front door: “Sorry, boss!”

“He can’t lie. It’s his worst quality. I asked him where his hoodie was. His ears went red. He said a man had borrowed it for an important mission.” She turned her cup. “Then he said, and I quote, Please don’t make me say more, Miss Lin, I have to live.”

He said nothing.

“Then Aurelia rang! Because Chen Si told her. Because Chen Si tells her everything. She laughed for ten minutes. She said you stood at the back of Miles Wei’s lecture for an hour and a half looking like someone had shot your dog.”

Nothing.

“So.” Elowen sipped her tea. “How was your meeting in the north?”

“Fifteen minutes. About nothing.”

“You made a meeting. So you wouldn’t be lying.”

“Yes.”

“And the lecture. Did you sit down at least?”

“I stood.”

“For an hour and a half.”

“At the back. By the door.”

“Like a bodyguard. For a quasar.”

“Hm.”

Her mouth was doing something. He couldn’t tell what yet.

He waited for it. The cold voice. The one she used on the man at the market who short-counted her roses. You promised.

She put her face in her hands.

Her shoulders started to shake. Was she crying? Oh no. Was she—

She was laughing.

It came up from somewhere deep. She put her head down on the counter next to the other FLOWER POWER hoodie and laughed till she was gasping. Till tears ran down her face. He stood in the doorway of his own kitchen and had no idea what to do with his hands.

“You— you borrowed a hoodie—”

“It was a disguise.”

That made it so much worse.

He came across the kitchen, slowly, and stood by her stool. After a while he put his hand on her back. She was still shaking with it under his palm.

“Was he good?” Into the counter, when she could talk. “The lecture?”

He thought about lying. He didn’t.

“Yes. Very good. He made a schoolgirl understand quasars. He dropped the clicker twice.” A pause. “He’s kind. He stops everything to answer a question. You were right about him.”

She lifted her head. Wet, pink face.

“And?”

“And he said sometimes you can’t see the heaviest thing in the middle. You only know it’s there because of how everything round it bends.”

She went quiet.

Why had he said that? He hadn’t planned to. He wanted it back immediately. He didn’t even know what it meant. Only that he’d stood at the back of that theatre thinking about a lemon tree and hadn’t been able to breathe properly for an hour.

She reached up and took his hand off her back and held it.

“Come to the reunion. Stand next to me. Meet him.”

“Why?”

“Because once you’ve stood next to him you’ll see there’s nothing to be jealous of. And you can stop reading his papers at two in the morning.”

Did he believe her? Not really. But she pulled him down by the hand and kissed him, slow, in the kitchen at midnight, with a teenager’s hoodie on the counter between them. He decided understanding could wait.

He lifted her off the stool. The hoodie slid onto the floor. He sat her on the counter and kissed her back, not slow at all, one hand in her hair and the other flat on the small of her back, until she’d forgotten she was laughing at him and had his shirt in both fists. “Three hundred people,” he said against her mouth. “And I was thinking about you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to bed in it.

Xiao Pan’s. Grey. Enormous on her. FLOWER POWER across her back. She climbed in and pulled the hood up and lay there looking smug.

“That’s Xiao Pan’s.”

“It’s evidence.”

“You have to give it back.”

“Tomorrow. Maybe. Mm… no.” She turned over and put her cold feet on his shins. He hissed. “It’s mine now. You can borrow it for your next lecture.”

“There won’t be a next lecture.”

“Mm-hm.”

“Elowen.”

She was already asleep. Or pretending. With her, you never knew.

He lay there with her feet on his legs and her hood in his face.

“Elowen.”

“Mm.”

“Did you like it? The library. The quiet.”

She didn’t open her eyes. She found his hand under the duvet and pulled it over onto her stomach, on top of FLOWER POWER, and held it there.

“I like this,” she said. “Go to sleep. You’ve had a very big night. You were a student.”

He lay awake a while. He kept his hand exactly where she’d put it.

chapters.title: The Reunion, Table Nine
chapters.desc: The reunion. Aurelia fixes Miles's bow tie, Miles asks Elowen if she's happy, and then he walks up to the man by the wall without knowing who he is.
chapters.epigraph: “Chen Si, look after your brother. He looks like he wants to check the exits.”
chapters.content:
In the car, she grabbed his tie and yanked it straight.

“Ow.”

“It was crooked.”

“You did it on purpose.”

“I did it so Aurelia can’t.” She smoothed it flat against his chest. Then she left her hand there a second longer than the tie needed. “Don’t let her touch your tie. She’ll tell everyone she dressed you.”

“Hm.”

He was looking at the red dress. He’d been looking at it since the top of the stairs. He’d said nothing about it. Not one word. On the steps he’d stopped and just stood there with his car keys in his hand until Bao coughed.

“Say something.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because then we won’t get there.”

Her face went hot all the way to her mother’s pearl earrings. Bao, in the front, turned the radio on.

✦ ✦ ✦

The ballroom at the Harbour Hotel had been decorated by someone who thought sixty years meant as much gold as possible.

Gold chairs. Gold tablecloths. A gold balloon arch over the door with the school crest on it, going soft on one side. Two hundred former students in evening dress under the chandeliers, holding champagne and pretending not to check who’d got fat.

Elowen stopped in the doorway with her hand on her husband’s arm.

She felt it go through the room. Out from the door, like a ripple. Heads turning. Talk stopping. People who hadn’t thought about Lin Elowen in seven years looking at her in red. Then at the man beside her.

She’d expected whispers. The Ice Queen. Didn’t she marry… isn’t that…?

She hadn’t expected them to step back.

But they did. A little. Without knowing they were doing it. The crowd near the door eased away from him like the market did when he walked in. He wasn’t doing anything. He was standing there in a black suit with his hands at his sides, looking up at the balloon arch with mild, polite confusion.

“Why is everything gold?”

“Aurelia was on the committee.”

“Ah.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came down the three steps into the ballroom on Chen Si’s arm like they were palace steps. Gold dress. Gold at her throat. Gold in her ears. She matched the ceiling exactly. The room turned to look. She let it.

Then she saw Elowen. And stopped dead on the bottom step.

She crossed the ballroom in a straight line. People got out of her way too. Differently.

“You wore RED.”

“Hello, Aurelia.”

“To my reunion.”

“Our reunion.”

“Everyone’s in black or gold! I planned it! You’re the only red thing in the room. You look like a… like a stop sign. A gorgeous stop sign.” Aurelia’s eyes narrowed and slid to Zhao. “You did this.”

Zhao said nothing.

“He bought five.”

“Five?” Aurelia looked at him with new respect. Then she reached for his tie.

Zhao stepped back.

Aurelia’s hand stayed in the air. She looked at the tie. At Elowen. At the tie again. Straight. Perfect.

“Oh, you witch.”

“Table nine?”

“Table nine.” Aurelia hooked her arm through Elowen’s. “Chen Si. Look after your brother. He looks like he wants to check the exits.”

“He’s checked them.” Chen Si had his phone out. It was buzzing. He frowned at it. “Twice. There are four. One’s a kitchen.” He lifted the phone. “Excuse me. Two minutes.”

It was not two minutes. He was out in the corridor for most of the first course.

✦ ✦ ✦

Miles Wei arrived late.

He came in through the kitchen door. Of course he did. He stood blinking at the gold balloons with a folder of notes held to his chest like a shield. A dinner suit that didn’t fit. A bow tie that had been tied, very confidently, by a man who understood light and not knots.

He was exactly the same and completely different. Taller. Thinner. Dark-framed glasses now. He still stood a bit hunched, like he was sorry for taking up the height.

Then he saw her.

She watched him recognise her. Surprise. Something warmer. And then his eyes moved to Aurelia beside her, and his face filled with such pure schoolboy alarm that Elowen laughed out loud.

She saw his mouth make the words across the ballroom. Oh no. Both of them.

He came over anyway. He was brave like that.

“Elowen. Aurelia.” He looked from one to the other. “You’re… you’re standing next to each other. On purpose.”

“We’re grown women now, Miles.” Aurelia, sweetly. “We save the shouting for galas.” Her eyes dropped to his neck. “Your bow tie is crooked.”

“Is it? I followed a diagram—”

She was already fixing it. Three sharp movements. Tug. Tug. Flat. Done.

Elowen looked very hard at the balloon arch and did not watch.

“There. Now you look like you know what a party is.”

“I don’t. Really.” He touched the bow tie like it might bite.

He turned to say something to Elowen. He never got to. The head teacher swooped out of nowhere, all sequins and lanyard, and took him by the elbow.

“There you are. Top table, Dr. Wei, you’re with us, come, come, the slides…”

And he was gone. Towed away across the ballroom with his folder, looking back over his shoulder like a man being taken out to sea.

Zhao had watched the whole thing from three metres back, by the pillar.

He hadn’t come any closer. He hadn’t been introduced. Miles had never once looked at him.

“Is that him?”

“That’s him.”

“Hm.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was strange.

Aurelia talked. Chen Si came back from the corridor and sat down.

“Who was it?” Aurelia, without turning her head.

“Work.”

“At my reunion.”

“Our reunion,” said Elowen and Chen Si, at exactly the same time.

Aurelia threw a bread roll at nobody in particular. After that Chen Si listened to Aurelia. Elowen hardly ate. Zhao sat beside her and ate everything and said nothing at all, with his arm along the back of her chair.

“What does your husband do, Elowen?” A woman from their year. Pearls. Very interested.

“Import and export.”

Chen Si coughed into his napkin.

When Aurelia told the story of Elowen correcting the head teacher’s maths in front of the whole school, Zhao turned his head and looked at his wife. Just looked. With no guard on his face at all. The woman in pearls put her fork down and didn’t pick it up again.

Then the lights went down. Miles went up to the lectern with his folder and a clicker.

He was good.

He was nervous for about a minute, and then he forgot to be. He talked about light. How it bends round heavy things. Two hundred people who’d slept through physics went quiet and listened. Halfway through, he dropped the clicker. He went down after it, still talking. A slide of a galaxy bent into a ring sat on the screen above the empty lectern while his voice came from underneath.

“…sorry. Sorry. It’s fine. The universe is still there.”

The whole ballroom laughed.

Elowen watched him. The library. The quiet. A boy explaining why the sky was blue.

What did she feel? She checked. Carefully. A sort of soft fondness. Like a house you lived in when you were small. Grateful. A bit sad. And very glad you didn’t live there any more.

She turned her head.

Zhao wasn’t watching Miles.

He was watching her. He had been the whole time.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the speech she went out onto the balcony for air.

The ballroom was too hot and too gold and too full of people asking what her husband did. Out here it was cold and dark. The harbour below. Ships’ lights crawling over black water.

Behind her, inside, Zhao had taken up a place by the wall where he could see the balcony door. She could feel him there without turning round.

The door opened.

“You left before the head teacher’s speech.”

Miles. He’d taken his bow tie off. Aurelia would be livid. He had two glasses of water and gave her one.

“I never stay for speeches. Only my own. And I don’t really want to stay for those either.”

He came and leaned on the rail beside her. A comfortable distance away. It had always been easy to be quiet with Miles. That had been the whole point.

“You were good.”

“I dropped the clicker.”

“Everyone loved that part.”

“That’s what worries me.”

They stood there a while.

“Can I ask you something?”

“Yes.”

He looked at the water. He turned the glass in his hands.

“Are you happy?”

Not how are you. Not how’s the shop. Just that. The way he asked about galaxies. Because he wanted the answer, not because he’d already decided what it should be.

She opened her mouth to say what she always said. Yes, of course. The shop’s doing well.

Nothing came out.

Nobody had ever asked her. Not once. Not Baba, not her teachers, not anyone. Was she? How would she even know? She stood on the cold balcony with the glass of water in her hand, and had to actually stop and think.

The market at four in the morning with two coffees waiting. A man in a too-short green apron, bleeding on roses. A lemon tree with five lemons. A note taped to a wall underground. This light stays on. A mountain in the rain. A hoodie that said FLOWER POWER.

“Yes.” And then, hearing it, surprised by it: “Yes. I am.”

Miles smiled at the harbour. His old crooked smile. The one he’d given her across the library table when she finally cracked a problem.

“Good. You used to talk about getting on a train. Every week. To the end of the line.”

“I’d forgotten that.”

“I hadn’t.” He drank his water. “You don’t look like you want to get on a train any more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the other side of the glass, Zhao stood by the wall and watched them.

He couldn’t hear a word. He saw his wife at the rail in red. He saw the thin man beside her, closer than anybody but Aurelia had stood to her all night. He saw the man say something. He saw Elowen go still and think about it. Then say something. Then smile.

He saw the man smile back.

Something cold went through him and settled in his stomach.

“Zhendong.” Chen Si, at his elbow. “Whatever you’re thinking…”

“I’m not thinking anything.”

“You’re thinking about the balcony.”

“There’s a balcony?”

“Zhendong.”

“Hm.”

The balcony door opened. Miles Wei came back in alone. Empty glass. Still a bit out of breath from the speech, or from the cold, or from whatever he’d just decided. He looked round the ballroom. He saw the big man in black by the wall.

He didn’t know who he was. He’d never been told. He just knew it was the man who’d been watching the balcony door all night.

He walked straight over.

“Excuse me.”

Zhao looked at him.

“Sorry. I don’t… I’m not very good at…” A vague wave at the balloons. The people. All of it. “This. But.”

He pushed his glasses up his nose.

“She doesn’t look like she wants to run.”

Zhao didn’t move. He didn’t say anything at all. He looked at Miles Wei for about four seconds, flat and unblinking.

Miles nodded, like he’d finished a lecture. He turned round and walked directly into a waiter with a tray of champagne.

In the noise and the glass, Chen Si leaned toward his brother.

“Well. He’s braver than he looks.”

Zhao didn’t answer. He was looking at the balcony door.

✦ ✦ ✦

When Elowen came in from the cold, pink-cheeked and bright-eyed, he’d crossed the ballroom before she’d taken three steps.

He took her hand. So hard she looked up.

Then he bent his head and stopped, his mouth a breath from hers, in the middle of the ballroom. His eyes were black. His jaw was tight. Jealous. He wasn’t hiding it. And he’d stand there like that all night, in front of everybody, if she didn’t answer.

So she closed the last centimetre herself.

In front of two hundred former students and every teacher who’d ever called her the Ice Queen, he kissed her back. Not long. Hard enough that she had to hold on to his sleeve.

“What?” When she could talk. “What happened?”

He didn’t answer. He just held on.

They didn’t dance. He didn’t know how. But he didn’t let go of her hand once for the rest of the night. Not during the head teacher’s speech. Not during the photograph. When she stood to watch the cake come in, he stood behind her with both arms round her and his chin on her hair.

Aurelia, across table nine, mouthed disgusting and took a photo.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car she slipped her heels off and put her stockinged feet in his lap. He wrapped one big hand round both of them. They were freezing.

“What did Miles say to you? Aurelia says he marched up to you and then walked into a waiter.”

Zhao looked out at the harbour for a while.

“That you don’t look like you want to get on a train.”

She was quiet.

“I don’t.”

“Good.” His thumb went over the arch of her foot. “If you did, I’d buy the railway.”

“Zhendong.”

“A small one. Just the line to the end.”

She laughed so hard Bao turned the radio up.

“You were jealous.”

“Yes.”

“Of Miles.”

“It’s ridiculous.” He didn’t look at her. “He’d lose a fight to a coat stand.”

“He would. He absolutely would.”

“I know.”

He was still holding her feet when they pulled up at the house. He carried her heels up the steps in one hand. He carried her in the other, because she said the gravel was too cold, and he didn’t argue.

chapters.title: Two Women, One Gala, Zero Ceasefire
chapters.desc: The Chen Foundation gala. Qiu Wen touches her peonies and she asks after his brother's hands. Then Zhao dances, very badly, on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “Floral is a tablecloth. Jewellery is a crown.” “Jewellery is a rock someone dug out of a hole.” — overheard, Chen Foundation Spring Gala
chapters.content:
“You can’t mean me.”

“I mean exactly you.” Aurelia on the phone, two months before. “The Chen Foundation Spring Gala. Chen Si’s people run everything. I run the flowers. And I want the best florist in the city.”

“Since when do you think I’m the best florist in the city?”

“Since never. I’ll deny it. And then I’m going to stand next to every arrangement all night and tell people exactly how I’d have done it differently.”

It was the most expensive night of the year. Officially it raised money for the children’s hospital. Unofficially, it was where the people who ran the city came to look at each other. Developers. Port officials. Two judges. A deputy mayor. And a man from the provincial security bureau, at a table near the stage, very carefully not looking at the table where Chen Si sat.

“Everyone goes. Some of them because they’re scared not to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dress came a week before. A flat white box from a shop on Harbour Road. Deep blue silk, cut close, her size exactly. Under it, in a smaller box, long earrings. Sapphires, the blue of the dress, in white gold.

She found him in the kitchen cutting spring onions and held them up by their hooks.

“How did you know my size?”

“Aurelia.” He didn’t stop cutting. “She said blue.”

She’d been planning to wear the red again. One of the five. If she was honest, she’d been planning to make a small point of wearing the red again. She stood in the kitchen with more than the shop made in a season hanging off her fingers, and found she didn’t want to make the point any more.

She wanted to see his face when she came down the stairs.

So she wore the blue.

When she came down he was halfway into his coat. He stopped with one arm in it. He let the coat fall on the floor. He came to the bottom of the stairs and took her hand as she reached the last step, and turned it over, and put his mouth on the inside of her wrist. He stayed there till she felt her own pulse jump against his lips.

She tipped her face up for the rest.

He looked at her mouth. He didn’t take it.

“Later. Ask me in the car.”

Then he stood there and didn’t move toward the door at all.

“Zhendong. We’ll be late.”

“Yes.”

“Your coat’s on the floor.”

“Yes.”

Bao, holding the front door, had a very long look at the ceiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

“The peonies are leaning.”

“They’re reaching for the light.” Elowen moved a stem one millimetre. “You wouldn’t know. You only work with things that are already dead.”

Aurelia touched the diamond collar at her throat.

“Says the woman wearing my sapphires.” She smiled at Elowen’s ears. “He came into my shop on a Tuesday. Pointed at the case. Asked if it came in blue. I charged him double. He didn’t even blink.”

Elowen had not known where they came from. She didn’t let it show.

“Diamonds are rocks. Peonies grow back.”

They stood in the middle of the ballroom in front of the biggest arrangement Elowen had ever made. A two-metre column of white peonies, gold-leafed branches and trailing jasmine. All around them the gala swirled in black and silver. People stopped to look at the flowers. Then at the two women beside them. One in blue silk. One in gold. Both smiling with every tooth they had.

“Do they always do this?” the deputy mayor asked at the bar.

Chen Si didn’t even look round. “Every time. It’s how they say hello.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the bar, Zhao drank water and watched the room.

That was how it went at these things. Chen Si worked the room. Zhao watched it. Who came in with whom. Who looked at the exits. Who had something under their jacket that wasn’t a wallet.

The deputy mayor had a bodyguard. Not a good one. The security bureau man had two. Good ones. A developer by the window was already drunk and would need taking home before the speeches.

And by the side door, the one the waiters used, a man in a grey suit had just come in with a woman on his arm.

Old white scar on the back of his left hand. Round. About the size of a coin.

Zhao put his water down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Qiu Wen had changed.

Nearly a year ago he’d stood at the edge of the old road with his warehouse burning and his brother on the ground with blistered hands. You’re a dead man, Zhao. He’d been fat then. Loud. Gold chains. A car with no lights.

Now he was thin. Good suit. Expensive haircut. The woman on his arm was an actress off a billboard by the Docks. He walked into the Chen Foundation Spring Gala like he’d been invited. He looked round the room, slow. He found Zhao at the bar.

He smiled.

Then he looked past Zhao, at the centre of the room. At the column of white peonies. At the woman in blue beside them, laughing at something Aurelia had said.

Zhao was moving before he’d decided to.

He didn’t hurry. Hurrying made people look. He went along the edge of the room. Past the bar. Past the deputy mayor’s bad bodyguard. Past the drunk developer. He arrived beside his wife at the exact same moment Qiu Wen did.

“Mrs. Zhao.” Pleasant. “What beautiful flowers.”

Elowen turned.

She’d never seen Qiu Wen. Or had she? She’d seen two black shapes running at the end of her street with the van on fire behind them. But she saw her husband’s face. And Aurelia’s. And she knew.

“Thank you.” Her wedding-card voice.

“I’ve always loved peonies.” He reached out and touched one. The hand with the scar. “So delicate. So easy to bruise.” He turned the flower toward him. “You have to be careful where you keep them, don’t you? I hear even a little heat can ruin them.”

Aurelia’s smile didn’t move. Her glass of water went down on a passing waiter’s tray without her looking. Her fingers closed round her little gold clutch, which plainly had more than lipstick in it.

Zhao didn’t move. He just looked at Qiu Wen.

Elowen got there first.

She reached out and took Qiu Wen’s hand off her peony. Firmly. The way she took customers’ hands off the display buckets. She let it go.

“You’re right. They bruise easily. That’s why I never let anyone touch them who doesn’t know what he’s doing.” She smiled. “Your brother must have told you all about heat, Mr. Qiu. How are his hands?”

Nobody breathed. Was Aurelia going to shoot him? Was Zhendong?

Qiu Wen’s smile stayed exactly where it was. His eyes changed. He looked at her properly for the first time. The way men in her father’s kitchen used to look at her when they realised she’d been listening the whole time.

“Healing. Slowly.”

“Cold water. Twenty minutes. I’m told it helps.”

Behind her, Aurelia made a noise that might have been a laugh.

Qiu Wen inclined his head. He gave Zhao one last long flat look. This isn’t over. Then he took the actress’s arm and walked off into the crowd.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao let out a breath.

“You shouldn’t have done that.” Low.

“He touched my flowers.”

“He was threatening you.”

“I know.” Her hands were shaking. She hid them in the folds of the dress. “So I answered him.”

Aurelia picked a fresh glass of champagne off a tray and pushed it into Elowen’s hand. She took a water for herself. She never drank champagne at these things. Chen Si’s people made sure no glass reached her that hadn’t come from him.

“Darling. I take back everything I said about the peonies.” Clink. “And I’m telling Chen Si to find out exactly who brought that man into this room. And then I’m going to ruin their entire life.”

“You can’t do that.”

“I absolutely can. I did the seating. I have a list.” She held out her hand. “Phone.”

“Why?”

“Phone, Elowen!”

Elowen gave her the phone. Aurelia scrolled. Her thumb stopped.

“Who’s this? Who is this number with no name that you’ve texted forty times this week?”

“Give it back.”

“Is this your HUSBAND? You saved your husband as nothing?”

“Give it—”

“He bought you a mountain!” Aurelia was typing. Fast. “There. That’s Chen Si. For emergencies, darling. The real kind.” She handed it back. “And save your husband. It’s embarrassing for all of us.”

Elowen put the phone in her bag without looking at it. Her ears were burning.

Zhao had heard every word. Not a sound out of him. He looked very slightly pleased with himself, which was worse.

When Aurelia had swept off to find her husband, he bent his head.

“Your hands.”

She brought them out of the silk. He took both of them in one of his, right there in the middle of the ballroom. In front of the deputy mayor and two judges and the man from the security bureau. He held them against his chest till they stopped shaking.

“You took his hand off your flowers.” His thumb went over her knuckles. “Next time he touches anything of yours, I’ll take the hand off for you.”

“That’s not funny.”

“No.” He turned her hands over like he was checking for damage. “You scared him. I watched his eyes.” A pause. “Do it somewhere with fewer judges next time. So I can kiss you after.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He found the man who’d put Qiu Wen on the list in the corridor by the cloakroom.

A port official. Small. Damp. He’d been paid. He started explaining before Zhao had said anything. Qiu Wen was a businessman now. A donor. He’d made a generous gift to the hospital. It was a charity gala, Mr. Zhao, anyone could—

“How much?”

The man told him.

Zhao nodded. He took the man’s coat off the cloakroom hook himself and held it out for him, like a waiter.

“Go home.”

“I… the speeches haven’t…”

“Go home. Go out the kitchen.” He put the coat round the man’s shoulders and did up the top button for him. Neatly. Carefully. “Don’t come back next year. Or the year after.”

The man went out through the kitchen. Nobody at the Chen Foundation saw him again.

Zhao went back in and checked his watch. Eleven minutes. He’d missed nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later the band played something slow.

Couples drifted onto the floor under the chandeliers. Chen Si took Aurelia’s hand without asking. She rolled her eyes and let him. They went across the floor like two people who’d done this for years and had never once agreed who was leading.

Elowen watched them from the edge.

“I don’t dance.”

“I know.”

He looked at the floor. Chen Si turning Aurelia under his arm. The deputy mayor treading on his wife’s feet. All the people who’d stepped back from him in doorways his whole life.

Then he held out his hand.

“You’ll have to lead. I’ll follow. I’m good at instructions.”

She took it.

He was terrible. Truly terrible. He had no idea what to do with his feet. He held her at arm’s length, carefully, like the first box of eucalyptus at the market. Every time she tried to move him he went the wrong way. He trod on her hem twice. Turning, they bumped right into Chen Si and Aurelia.

“Oh, for heaven’s sake…”

“Leave them, my queen.” Chen Si steered her off.

Elowen started to laugh.

“Closer. You’re not carrying me. You’re dancing with me.”

He came closer. Her cheek ended up on his shoulder. His hand spread wide on her back, warm through the silk. They gave up on feet altogether and just swayed in a small circle, while the chandeliers turned and the most dangerous people in the city watched the arms dealer and the florist rock back and forth in the middle of the floor like two kids at a school dance.

“You said you don’t dance.”

“I’m not dancing.” Into her hair. “I’m holding you in public. It’s different.”

She shut her eyes and leaned into him.

Over by the side door, Qiu Wen stood in the dark with a drink he hadn’t touched, watching them.

Zhao saw him. He kept swaying. He kept hold of her. He looked at Qiu Wen over the top of his wife’s head, steady, until the other man looked away first.

Then he put two fingers under her chin and tipped her face up and kissed her. Slow. In the middle of the floor, under the chandeliers. In front of both judges and the deputy mayor and the man from the security bureau. So that Qiu Wen and everybody else in the room would know exactly whose she was.

“So much for the judges,” she said against his mouth.

“Hm.”

He kept dancing. Badly.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the end of the night, in the cold at the top of the hotel steps, Aurelia pulled on her gloves and sighed.

“Next New Year we’re doing it properly. A real table. Not four people and a takeaway.” She frowned at the glove. “Where, though? Where does anyone go?”

Elowen looked at her. Then she looked past her, through the glass doors, to where Zhao and Chen Si stood side by side by the wall with their hands in their pockets. Not speaking. Waiting for their wives like two guard dogs who’d agreed to share a gate.

“You might as well come,” she said coolly. “Next year. To the Lins’. He’ll only sulk if you don’t.”

Aurelia stopped with one glove half on.

“Who will?”

Elowen didn’t even look round.

“Both of them.”

chapters.title: The Question He Almost Asks
chapters.desc: In the car home, he gets as far as her name. A year to the day, a fourteenth key. Then the phone rings at three.
chapters.epigraph: “The code is for if something happens. The key is for if you just want to come in.”
chapters.content:
She fell asleep in the car before they’d even left the hotel drive.

One minute she was telling him the peonies had leaned because the ballroom was too hot, and it was Aurelia’s fault, obviously. The next her head dropped onto his shoulder and stayed there.

Zhao sat up straight. He didn’t move his arm. It went numb at the harbour. He didn’t move it then either. Bao drove like the car was full of eggs.

Her hair smelled of jasmine from the big arrangement. A gold leaf off one of the branches had got caught above her ear. He looked at it. He left it there.

At the first red light he turned his face into her hair and breathed in. Just once. Like a man coming up from deep water. The light went green. Bao didn’t move off for a second. Then he did.

Qiu Wen’s hand on the white peony. So easy to bruise. Her hand taking it off. Firm. The way she took a customer’s hand off the buckets. How are his hands?

The physics boy at the reunion, out of breath, holding an empty glass. She doesn’t look like she wants to run.

And under all of that, where it always was, her father at the dining table. She didn’t choose you. She chose me. You were only the price she paid.

He’d carried that sentence around for months. Like a stone in a shoe. He’d stopped noticing it most days. Tonight he noticed it.

“Elowen.”

He hadn’t meant to say it out loud.

“Mm?”

Her eyes stayed shut. Her mouth was a bit open. In the front, Bao’s hands had gone very still on the wheel.

“When you married me…”

He stopped.

When you married me, was it only for him? If he hadn’t lost three containers, would you have looked at me twice? Do you ever think about the other bus?

“What about it?” she mumbled, into his sleeve.

The car hit a bump. She sighed. Pushed her face harder into his shoulder. Then her hand came up in her sleep and grabbed a fistful of his shirt. Hard. Like he might get out at the next light. He looked down at her fingers. Knuckles white. Asleep, and still holding on.

“Nothing. Go back to sleep.”

She did. Bao cleared his throat.

“Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything, boss.”

“You were going to.”

Bao drove the rest of the way home with his mouth shut so hard his jaw clicked.

At the house Zhao lifted her out without waking her. Up the steps. Past the lemon tree. Up the stairs to their room. He laid her on the bed in the blue silk and took off her shoes. Then the earrings. Aurelia’s sapphires. He’d never taken an earring out of anything in his life. The first one took him a whole minute. She frowned in her sleep and turned her head to give him the other one. He nearly laughed. He put them in the glass vase on her side of the bed, next to the heavy ring she’d pulled off in the car because her fingers were swollen. Then he took the gold leaf out of her hair. Finally. He put that in the vase too.

Then he went down to the basement and sat at the bench until four. When it was time to drive her to the market.

✦ ✦ ✦

The anniversary was on a Wednesday. He’d forgotten. Obviously. He drove her to the market at four like always. Carried the buckets. Said nothing about anything. She said nothing back. She was fine about it. Totally fine.

Granny Su looked at the two of them over her lily of the valley.

“One year, hm?”

“How do you even know that?”

“You came here in a wedding dress with soil on your hands.” Granny Su stuffed an extra bunch into Elowen’s order. “Who forgets that?”

Elowen looked at her husband. He was reading the price of eucalyptus like it was a newspaper. Some people, apparently.

At the shop, Xiao Pan was less subtle.

“Miss Lin. Miss Lin. Is it today?”

“Is what today.”

“The thing. One year.” He looked over at Zhao, who was on the egg stool behind the counter eating his fried eggs. Then back at her. He lowered his voice to a whisper you could have heard across the harbour. “Does he know?”

“Xiao Pan. Buckets.”

“Because if he doesn’t, I could, like, accidentally mention—”

“Buckets.”

He went. Zhao finished his eggs. He washed the plate in her little sink, dried it, put it back exactly where it lived. He kissed the top of her head on his way out. Same as every morning. Nothing.

She stood there with the scissors in her hand. Fine. Good. She’d planned this for a month and she didn’t need him to remember anything. That was the whole point.

She’d gone back to the Greenstone hills in February, while he was down in the south. Two days on her own. Well. On her own plus Bao, because Bao was always somehow just there, on the next bench, reading a paper upside down. She’d gone to see the camellia in Mr. Wen’s walled garden. And when she left, the old man had pressed something into her hands, wrapped in rice paper.

One camellia flower. Deep pink. Pressed flat in a book, every petal lying perfectly over the last. For the husband. Tell him I said he’s an idiot. A good one.

It was in a thin black frame now, from the framer in the old town, between two panes of glass. Wrapped in brown paper. Hidden behind the ribbon on the back shelf for three weeks. She’d checked it every morning. Like a lunatic.

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave it to him that night. At the table. After the fish.

He unwrapped it slowly. He took the brown paper off and folded it into a square, because he folded everything of hers, and then he held the frame in both hands and didn’t say anything.

“Mr. Wen says you’re an idiot. A good one.”

He didn’t smile. He was looking at the flower.

“You went back. On your own.”

“In February. When you were away. Bao came.” She pointed her chopsticks at him. “How do you do that? I didn’t even tell him. I got to the bus station and he was already buying two tickets.”

“Hm.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“No.”

He put the frame down beside his bowl. Face up. Very carefully. Like it might spill. Then he reached into his jacket.

He put a key on the table in front of her. Small. Plain steel. A little red tag on a loop of string. She looked at it. Then at him.

“The fourteenth key.”

The basement. The steel door. The one he’d kept back on the first day, when he’d given her the ring of thirteen with their coloured tags and said she didn’t need that one.

“You gave me the code. The first night. I don’t need a key.”

“I know.” He didn’t look away from her. “The code is for if something happens. If you have to hide.” He pushed it a centimetre closer with one finger. “The key is for if you just want to come in.”

She picked it up. It was warm from his pocket.

“There’s nothing in this house you can’t open now.” His voice was flat. Like always. “I wanted you to have all of them.”

She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. Not one word. So he had remembered. All day. Eggs. Buckets. Kiss on the head. And he’d been carrying a key around in his jacket the whole time, letting her think he’d forgotten.

“You’re a terrible person.”

“Yes.”

“I was so sad at the market.”

The corner of his mouth went. Just barely. “I know. Granny Su told me to stop being cruel.”

“She knew?”

“Everybody knew. Xiao Pan nearly cried.”

She threw a fish bone at him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him upstairs. She didn’t say anything. She stood up and held out her hand. He took it. She walked him up the stairs and down the corridor to their room. She dropped the key in the glass vase with the sapphires and the gold leaf. It clinked.

He reached for her. She caught both his hands and stopped them.

“Let me.”

He let her.

Shirt first. One button at a time. Then she ran out of patience and yanked his tie loose from his collar, hard enough that he rocked forward a step. He made a noise in his throat. She folded the shirt anyway, neatly, and put it on the chair. He watched her do it. His breathing had gone rough.

“You’re folding it.”

“You fold mine.”

“That’s different.”

“How?”

He didn’t have an answer. She pushed him backwards onto the bed. He went down easily. Flat on his back. Looking up at her in the orange light off the Docks.

She climbed up and knelt over him. She took his wrists and put them above his head, on the pillow, one on top of the other.

“Don’t move.”

His eyes went black.

“Elowen.”

“Page two. Line six.” She bent down till her mouth was an inch from his. “You don’t touch me unless I ask. I’m not asking. Not yet. So don’t move.”

He didn’t move.

It was nearly killing him. She could see it. Good. She kissed him the way he always kissed her. Slow. Like she had all night and had decided to use every minute of it. His mouth. His jaw. The pulse in his throat, going so hard she felt it on her lips. The scar on his collarbone. The bullet scar on his shoulder. The long ridge down his ribs from Block C, all the way.

His hands had made fists in the pillow. When she got to the end of the scar, above his hip, and just stayed there, he said her name through his teeth like she’d burned him.

“Elowen. Please.”

She lifted her head. The most frightening man in the city. Flat on his back with his fists over his head because she’d told him to keep them there. Saying please.

Oh, she was never letting him forget this.

“Again.”

“Please.”

“Please what?”

He told her. Low and rough, staring up at her, he told her exactly what he wanted, and every word of it went straight down her spine. Her face went hot. Her whole body went hot. She sat back on her heels and looked at him for a second. Then she smiled.

“Okay. You can move.”

He moved.

✦ ✦ ✦

It wasn’t careful. Not like the first time, or the mountain. A year was in it. A year of learning exactly what made him lose his breath and exactly how long to make him wait for it. He rolled her under him in one go and kissed her so hard her head pushed back into the pillow. She laughed into his mouth.

Then she couldn’t laugh, because his hands were everywhere, greedy and sure, and he was talking against her skin. Low. Half words. Mine. You’re mine. Say it.

“Yours.” Her voice cracked on it. “Yours, Zhendong, yours—”

“Again.”

“You’re so bossy when—oh.”

He’d found the place under her ear. He wasn’t leaving it.

She stopped trying to have opinions. She hooked her leg round him to pull him down. She bit his shoulder to keep from making a noise. He laughed, rough and helpless. Then he wasn’t laughing either. He said her name into her neck over and over in the voice she only ever heard in this bed. Elowen. Elowen. At the end she held his face in both hands so she could watch it come apart.

This. She thought it very clearly. This is what I picked.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay on his chest in the dark. His heart was still going like a drum under her ear. His hand was spread flat on her back. It was right there. In her mouth. She could taste it.

It isn’t a contract any more. It hasn’t been for ages. I love you.

She thought about her father at the dining table. She thought about Zhao telling Raiden yes, over a hole in the floor, when he didn’t know she was in the doorway. Till I know she’d say it even if I didn’t. Not like this. Not in bed, after. With a key in the vase. He’d think it was the key talking. He’d think it was gratitude.

When she said it, he wasn’t going to be able to mistake it for anything.

“Happy anniversary.”

His hand stopped on her back.

“I thought you’d forgotten.”

“I don’t forget.” Quiet. “Nine forty-one. You had soil under your nails. You smelled of eucalyptus.”

She lifted her head and looked at him. “Why would you know the minute?”

“There was a clock on the wall.” He was quiet for so long she thought that was it. “In case it was the only one. In case you changed your mind by lunch. I wanted to know exactly when it started.”

She put her face back down on his chest. Fast. So he wouldn’t see it.

“That’s the stupidest thing I’ve ever heard.”

“Hm.”

His thumb went up and down her spine. He was smiling. She could hear it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The phone rang at three. Not hers. His. The one on his side of the bed that four people in the world had the number for. It buzzed on the wood and he was sitting up with it at his ear before the second buzz.

“Si.”

She sat up with the sheet round her shoulders. In the light from the screen she watched his face go blank. Not calm. Blank. Like somebody had wiped it.

“When?”

A pause.

“Which ones?”

A longer pause.

“Does she know?”

She went cold all over.

“No. I’ll tell her.”

He hung up. He sat on the edge of the bed with his back to her and the phone in his hand.

“Zhendong?”

“Put the news on.”

She found the remote under a pillow. The television on the wall came on far too bright. The international channel. A woman at a desk. Behind her, big red letters. INTERPOL NOTICE.

And a photograph. A bad one. Long lens, years old. A younger man in a cheap suit next to a car at some port, half turned away. Her husband.

…a Red Notice issued tonight for a man described as one of the most significant illegal arms brokers in the region, following a United Nations panel report linking a network of shell companies to shipments into at least four conflict zones under embargo…

She stared at it. …Zhao Zhendong, twenty-six, believed to be based in the Iron Docks district… Then the weather. Sunny tomorrow. Light winds.

He put the phone down on the bedside table. Next to the vase. The sapphires, the gold leaf, the fourteenth key.

“It’s a request. Not a warrant.” Flat. Even. Reading it off a page. “It asks police in other countries to find me and hold me. Here, it doesn’t mean much. Not yet. Si has people in the right offices.” A pause. “But I can’t leave the country now. Everyone I do business with just watched that. And everyone who wants me gone watched it too.”

She looked at his back. The long white scar down his ribs, blue in the light off the screen.

“How many people want you gone?”

He didn’t answer straight away.

“After tonight? More.”

She moved across the bed. She put both arms round him from behind and pressed her cheek between his shoulder blades. He went stiff. Then his hand came up over both of hers, where they were locked over his heart. He held them there. Hard. Like he was holding a door shut.

“You still have to drive me to the market at four.”

A breath went out of him. Not quite a laugh. He turned her hand over against his chest and kissed her knuckles, one at a time.

“Wear a coat.”

chapters.title: A Red Notice With His Face on It
chapters.desc: A detective from her childhood walks into the shop. A UN report with a familiar name buried on page sixty.
chapters.epigraph: “Someone wants him gone, Elowen. People like that don’t check who’s standing next to him.” — Detective Song Wei Long
chapters.content:
The phone on his side of the bed rang eleven times the first night. She counted.

Three in the morning. Four. Six. He took it to the kitchen window every time and stood there with it at his ear. Yes. No. When. How many. By the end of the week he was going to the Docks before the market and coming back after midnight. He’d stopped sitting down to eat. The contract said you eat dinner. In her handwriting. Underlined.

He ate standing up at the counter. Or not at all.

On the fourth night she woke at two and his side was cold.

She knew where he’d be.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was at the bench in the basement, under the hanging lamp. Not cleaning anything. Nothing in pieces. Just sitting there with his hands flat on the wood. Like he was holding the bench down.

She came down the stairs with a bowl. Rice. The last of the braised pork. A fried egg on top, the way he ate it on the stool at the shop. She put it on the cloth between his hands, where the bits of a gun usually were. Chopsticks next to it, lined up with the edge.

He looked at it.

“I’m not hungry.”

“I didn’t ask.” She sat down on the bottom step and pulled her knees up under her pyjamas. “I’m going to sit here until it’s gone.”

“Elowen.”

“I’ve got all night. I’ve got a shop. I can sleep in the cooler.”

He picked up the chopsticks.

He ate all of it. Slowly, for once. When he’d finished he looked over at her on the step.

“You came down here at two in the morning to make me eat an egg.”

“You sat outside my door for a month. This is cheaper.”

Something in his face eased. Not much. Enough. He didn’t bring her the bowl. He came and sat on the step below hers, with his back against her shins. She put both hands in his hair.

He leaned back into her. Slowly. All that weight. Like he’d forgotten that was allowed and was checking.

“How bad is it?”

“Two buyers. Gone.” His eyes were shut. “A captain who suddenly remembered his engine needs repairs.”

“Does it?”

“No.”

She kept her fingers moving in his hair.

“You haven’t slept.”

“I’m sleeping now.”

“You’re sitting on a step.”

“Hm.”

He was asleep in about a minute. On a concrete step. With his head against her knee. She sat there until her feet went numb. She didn’t move.

Every night after that there was a bowl. Every night he ate it sitting down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the shop, people started looking.

Not most of them. Most of her customers didn’t watch the international news. And the ones who did didn’t connect a blurry man in a cheap suit with the big quiet husband who sometimes swept her floor. But some did.

A woman she’d done wedding flowers for two years ago came in, saw who was in the corner with the newspaper, went white, and walked straight out again. Bell and all.

The old man who bought chrysanthemums for his wife’s grave every Sunday didn’t come on Sunday.

Xiao Pan lasted two days.

“Miss Lin.”

“No.”

“I didn’t say anything!”

“You were going to.”

He looked over his shoulder at the corner. Zhao was reading the shipping pages. Upside down, as far as she could tell, because he was looking at the door.

Xiao Pan dropped his voice. “Is Mr. Zhao on the actual international news?”

“Xiao Pan.”

“Like, international? Like other countries can see him…?”

“Buckets.”

“Is he famous?”

Behind the paper, very flat, Zhao spoke.

“I can hear you.”

Xiao Pan made a noise like a stepped-on duck and disappeared into the cooler.

She didn’t laugh. She bit the inside of her cheek so hard it hurt.

That evening, locking up, she said it to the shutters.

“People are going to stop coming.”

“It’ll pass.” He didn’t look at her when he said it. “People forget.”

“Do they?”

He didn’t answer. He took the shutter pole out of her hands and pulled it down himself. Since when did he lock up? Since the photograph, apparently.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday a man walked in and didn’t buy anything.

Her age, about. Tall. Plain dark coat. A face so still it looked carved out of something. He stood inside the door and looked around. Buckets. Cooler. The second row of tulips, over the drain cover in the floor. He looked at each thing for exactly as long as it took to remember it.

Then he looked at her, and the carved face cracked a little.

“Lin Elowen.”

It took her a second.

A skinny boy with a buzz cut. Sitting on the wall between her family’s house in the Walled City and the policeman’s house next door. Eating an ice lolly. Refusing to come down even when his father shouted.

“Song Wei Long?”

“Detective Song.” He took a small leather wallet out of his coat and showed her the badge like it was a bus ticket. “I’m not here officially.”
